answer: HYPOTHESIS (answering "What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?"): Urban land use has influenced two distinct types of plant introductions, acting at different stages of the invasion process. (1) UNINTENTIONAL introductions (accidental arrivals with contaminated seed lots, trade and tourism) are the pathway most strongly shaped by urban land cover at the local establishment scale: their records are over-represented in and around urbanized plots (36.0% of Unintentional records fall in the 'Urban' habitat vs a 28.3% baseline of occupied plots, enrichment ratio 1.27; mean surrounding urban cover 0.33 vs 0.30; Gardening-vs-Unintentional difference chi2=3.84, p=0.05), and their share within occupied plots increases with urban cover in the 500 m buffer (+0.74 on the log-odds scale, 95% Wald CI [-0.27, +1.74], LRT p=0.14), a direction consistent across the 2009 500 m and 1000 m buffers but absent at the 50 m scale and for 1956 cover — pointing to contemporary, landscape-scale urbanization rather than the plot itself. These species form a phylogenetically clustered urban/ruderal assemblage (within-pathway patristic distance 183 vs 208 under 999 label permutations, p=0.001; Amaranthus, Erigeron, Symphyotrichum, Xanthium-type herbs) with the widest habitat ranges (2.72) and largest number of invaded plots (mean 9.5). (2) GARDENING introductions were influenced by urban land use at the introduction-effort scale over time, not at the local establishment scale: Catalonia-wide, ornamental introductions rose from 16.8% of all introductions before 1500 to 75.2% in 1985–2019 (the period coinciding with modern urban growth), yet established Gardening species are NOT concentrated near urban cover (urban.2009.500m coefficient -0.80, CI [-1.82, +0.22], LRT p=0.11; enrichment in Urban habitat 0.94) because ornamentals persist across many habitat types (they include 44% trees/shrubs). (3) AGRICULTURE/FORESTRY introductions show no urban influence: null urban effect (+0.09, CI [-2.54, +2.72], p=1.00) and they are strongly urban-avoiding (only 8.7% of records in Urban habitat, enrichment 0.31). In short: accidental/unintentional introductions were promoted by urban land use where they establish, gardening/ornamental introductions were promoted by urban land use in what is imported and planted (temporally), and agriculture/forestry introductions were not urban-influenced. IMPORTANT CAVEAT carried into the answer: no individual pathway-vs-urban coefficient reaches p<0.05 at plot level (n=191 occupied plots); the urban influence on Unintentional introductions is supported by convergent descriptive, model-based and phylogenetic evidence rather than a single significant test.

payload.hypothesis: Urban land use has influenced two types of plant introductions at different stages of the invasion process: (1) unintentional introductions (contaminated seed lots, trade, tourism) are the pathway most strongly influenced by urban land use at the local establishment scale — their records are over-represented in urbanized plots (36% of records in 'Urban' habitat vs 28.3% baseline, enrichment 1.27; Gardening-vs-Unintentional chi2=3.84, p=0.05), their share within occupied plots increases with urban cover in the surrounding 500–1000 m landscape (+0.74 log-odds per unit urban.2009.500m, 95% CI [-0.27, +1.74], LRT p=0.14, consistent at 500 m and 1000 m in 2009 but absent at 50 m and for 1956 cover, implying contemporary landscape-scale urbanization rather than the plot itself), and these species form a phylogenetically clustered urban/ruderal assemblage (within-pathway patristic distance 183 vs null 208, p=0.001) with the widest habitat ranges (2.72) and most invaded plots (mean 9.5). (2) Gardening/ornamental introductions were influenced by urban land use at the introduction-effort scale over time, not at local establishment: Catalonia-wide their share of new introductions rose from 16.8% (before 1500) to 75.2% (1985–2019, the period of modern urban growth), yet established gardening species are not concentrated near urban cover (urban.2009.500m coefficient -0.80, CI [-1.82, +0.22], p=0.11; Urban-habitat enrichment 0.94) because ornamentals persist across many habitats (44% trees/shrubs). (3) Agriculture/forestry introductions show no urban influence (coefficient +0.09, CI [-2.54, +2.72], p=1.00) and are urban-avoiding (only 8.7% of records in Urban habitat, enrichment 0.31). In short, urban land use promoted accidental/unintentional introductions where aliens establish, drove the temporal explosion of ornamental (gardening) introductions, and left agriculture/forestry introductions unaffected.
payload.workflow: Inspected all four files (temporal table and niche CSV are tab-separated with quoted headers; species CSV comma-separated; Newick tree with 81 tips matching phylo.tip.label 1:1). Detected perfect separation in ordinary binomial GLMs of pathway composition (habitat strata with all-or-nothing pathway occurrence) and therefore fitted Firth-penalized binomial GLMs (grouped-binomial hat-matrix correction) with Wald 95% CIs and likelihood-ratio p-values. Models: (a) presence of aliens on all 632 plots; (b) pathway composition (n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo out of n.total) on the 191 occupied plots with primary exposure urban.2009.500m controlling for elevation, habitat (10 levels), annual temperature/rainfall, log distance to road/stream; (c) sensitivity with urban.1956.500m, urban.2009.50m, urban.2009.1000m; (d) secondary models adding progressive landscape-change fractions; (e) residual Moran's I diagnostics (k=8 nearest neighbours, 199 permutations); (f) descriptive urban-habitat enrichment with chi2; (g) Catalonia-wide temporal pathway shares as separate descriptive corroboration; (h) species-level summaries on 77 unique species (4 duplicates dropped); (i) optional phylogenetic robustness via 999-permutation test of within-pathway mean patristic distance using a hand-parsed Newick tree. All outputs written to results/ (36 CSV tables + SUMMARY.md).
